MEDICAL BILLING

How to read an 835 ERA file, and find the lines a payer underpaid

The 835 is the electronic remittance advice: the file a payer sends to say what it paid, what it adjusted and why. Most practices never open it. Their system posts it, writes off the difference as a contractual adjustment, and moves on. That is exactly where a payer paying below your contract rate goes unnoticed.

Open the free 835 underpayment finder

What is in the file

An 835 is plain text. It is a list of segments, each ending in a terminator (usually ~) with fields separated by another character (usually *). The segments that matter for a practice:

SegmentWhat it tells you
BPRThe payment: total amount, method, and date. This is the deposit.
TRNThe trace or check number that ties the file to the bank deposit.
N1Who the payer is and who the payee is.
CLPOne claim: your patient control number, status, billed amount, paid amount and patient responsibility.
CASAn adjustment: a group code, a reason code and an amount.
SVCOne service line: procedure code, billed, paid and units.
AMTExtra amounts on a line, including the allowed amount when the payer sends it.
PLBProvider-level adjustments outside any claim: recoupments, interest, rebates.

A simplified layout for orientation. Payers vary, and not every payer sends every segment.

Reading the adjustments: CO, PR and the reason code

Each CAS carries a group and a reason. CO is a contractual obligation the practice writes off, PR is patient responsibility, OA is other, and PI is a payer-initiated reduction. The number after it is the Claim Adjustment Reason Code. A few that come up constantly:

CO-45  Charge exceeds the fee schedule (contractual write-off)
PR-1   Deductible
PR-2   Coinsurance
PR-3   Co-payment
CO-97  Bundled into another service
CO-50  Not medically necessary
CO-16  Missing information or billing error
CO-253 Sequestration reduction

Why CO-45 is where underpayments hide

CO-45 is expected on nearly every line, so it gets posted without a second look. But the size of it is the payer's decision. If your contract says a service pays $120 and the payer allowed $108, the write-off is $12 larger than it should be and looks exactly like a correct one. Nothing in a posting screen flags it, because nothing compares the allowed amount with your rate.

Working out the allowed amount for a line

When the payer sends an AMT with the allowed qualifier, use it. When it does not, the allowed amount is the line payment plus the patient responsibility, with any sequestration reduction added back. Then multiply your contract rate by the units and compare. A line that paid something and carries no adjustment other than the contractual write-off, patient responsibility or sequestration is a clean test. A line reduced for bundling or medical necessity is not, because its lower payment may be legitimate.

Denials, takebacks and whether the file adds up

Beyond underpayments, an 835 shows denied claims with a reason code you can act on: some are fixable and resubmittable, some need an appeal, some belong to another payer or the patient. It also shows provider-level adjustments in PLB, which change the deposit without appearing on any claim, and the totals should balance: charge less payment equals the adjustments on each claim, and the deposit equals claim payments less provider-level adjustments. A file that does not balance has usually been misread or is missing something.

Do it without doing the arithmetic

The 835 underpayment finder does all of the above in your browser: drop in the file, paste your contract rates (one line per code and rate), and it lists the lines allowed below contract, the denials with a usual next step, any takebacks, and whether the file balances, with an appeal worksheet you can download as CSV. With no fee schedule it compares each payer to its own usual amount for the same code and says plainly that this finds inconsistency, not a breach.

Check a remittance file

Common questions

What is an 835 file?

The X12 835 is the electronic remittance advice (ERA): the machine-readable version of the explanation of benefits a payer sends a provider. It lists each claim the payer processed, what was billed and paid, every adjustment with a group code and a reason code, and the total that was deposited. It is a plain text file made of segments separated by a terminator character, usually a tilde.

Where do I get the 835 for a payment?

From your clearinghouse or the payer's provider portal, usually under ERA or remittance downloads. Many practice management systems also keep the raw file. The PDF explanation of benefits is not an 835 and cannot be read this way.

What do CO-45 and PR-1 mean?

The first part is the group: CO is a contractual obligation the practice writes off, PR is patient responsibility, OA is other adjustments and PI is a payer-initiated reduction. The number is the Claim Adjustment Reason Code. CO-45 is the charge exceeding the fee schedule, which is the normal contractual write-off, and PR-1 is the patient deductible.

Why is CO-45 the one that hides underpayments?

Because it is expected on every line. A practice posting the payment writes the CO-45 amount off without looking at it, so a payer that allowed less than the contract rate produces a larger CO-45 that looks exactly like a correct one. The only way to see it is to compare the allowed amount per line with the rate in your own contract.

How do I work out the allowed amount from an 835?

Use the AMT segment with qualifier B6 when the payer sends it. When it is absent, the allowed amount is the line payment plus the patient responsibility adjustments, plus any sequestration reduction added back. Coordination of benefits and withholds make that inexact, so a flagged line is a question for the payer, not a proven breach.

What is a PLB segment?

A provider-level balance adjustment: an amount that sits outside every claim, such as an overpayment recovery, interest, a rebate or a late-charge fee, with a reason code. It changes the deposit without appearing on any claim, which is why a file can look correct claim by claim and still not match the money that arrived.

Is it safe to open an 835 in a web tool?

An 835 can contain protected health information. This tool reads the file in your browser, sends nothing anywhere and never reads patient names or member IDs into the page, but this is not a HIPAA compliance assessment. Follow your own policies about where PHI may be opened.

Is this billing, coding or legal advice?

No. It is arithmetic on the file and the rates you provide. Check any finding against the payer's own records and your contract before disputing a payment.

835 ERA UNDERPAYMENT FINDER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Did your payers pay what your contract says?

Drop in an X12 835 remittance file and get the service lines paid below your contract rates, denied claims with plain-language reasons and a next step, provider-level takebacks, and a check that the file adds up. Download the lot as a worksheet to work the appeals from.

The file is read in this browser tab and never leaves your device. Patient names and member IDs are never read into the page; claims are identified by your own patient control number. Independent of any payer or clearinghouse. The 835 layout is read by position from memory of the standard and no real remittance was available when this was built; if a file is not read, the page says which segments it could not.

1. Your remittance file(s)

Download the 835 (often .835, .txt, .edi or .era) from your clearinghouse or payer portal. You can choose several files at once. A PDF explanation of payment will not work; it has to be the electronic file.

2. Your contract rates (optional)

One line per code: 99213,92.50. A modifier can follow a dash: 99213-25,80. The rate is the allowed amount per unit. Leave this empty to compare each payer with its own usual amount instead.

Choose a file or paste the text, then click Analyze.

The model, and what it leaves out

  • Allowed amount for a line is the AMT allowed amount when the file carries one, otherwise payment plus patient responsibility, plus any sequestration reduction added back. Coordination of benefits, withholds and capitation make that inexact, so treat a flagged line as a question to put to the payer.
  • Underpaid means expected (your rate times units) minus allowed is above the tolerance. Only lines that paid something and carry no adjustment other than the contractual write-off, patient responsibility or sequestration are tested; the rest are counted as skipped.
  • Without a schedule the test is a payer against its own most common per-unit amount for a code (at least three clean lines, at least half agreeing). It finds inconsistency, not proof of a breach.
  • Denials are claims with status 4, or nothing paid and a non-patient adjustment. Reversals are not denials. Reason text is from memory and abbreviated; unknown codes are labelled unknown.
  • Balance checks test that charge less payment equals the listed adjustments on each claim and line, and that each deposit equals claim payments minus provider-level adjustments.
  • Not modelled: payer appeal deadlines, rates that change by date of service, place of service, plan or provider, multiple-procedure and bundling rules, secondary-payer logic, interest owed on late payment, and anything not in the file.

Common questions

How do I find out if an insurance payer underpaid my practice?

Drop the 835 electronic remittance file your clearinghouse or payer portal gives you into this page and paste your contract fee schedule (one line per CPT code and rate). The tool works out the amount each payer allowed on every service line, from the AMT allowed amount when the file has one or from payment plus patient responsibility when it does not, and lists the lines allowed below your contract rate by more than a tolerance you set. The file is read in your browser and never uploaded.

What if I do not have my contract rates handy?

Leave the schedule empty. The tool then compares each payer with its own most common allowed amount per unit for the same code, using only codes with at least three clean lines from that payer. That finds inconsistent pricing inside the file, but a legitimate difference such as place of service or plan looks identical, so treat those as questions to ask the payer, not as proof.

Is it safe to put an 835 file with patient information into a web page?

The page runs entirely in your browser: the file is read locally, nothing is sent anywhere, and a test in the code asserts there are no network calls. Patient names and member IDs are never read into the page's data; claims are identified by the patient control number your own system assigned. This is not a HIPAA compliance assessment. If your policies bar pasting PHI into any browser tool, run it from a downloaded copy of the page on an approved machine or do not use it.

Which lines does the underpayment check skip?

Lines that paid nothing, and lines carrying any adjustment other than the contractual write-off (CO-45), patient responsibility or sequestration (CO-253). A line reduced for bundling, a multiple-procedure rule or medical necessity is not a clean test of your contract rate, so it is counted as skipped rather than flagged.

What do the denial reason codes mean?

The tool translates the common Claim Adjustment Reason Codes into plain language and suggests a usual next step: resubmit with a fix, appeal, check the contract, bill another payer or bill the patient. The list is written from memory and abbreviated, so a code it does not know is shown as unknown rather than guessed. Payer-specific remark codes are not read.
